title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #180: Turán Numbers for Graph Families**

For a finite family $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs, does some $G \in \mathcal{F}$ have $\mathrm{ex}(n; G) = O(\mathrm{ex}(n; \mathcal{F}))$?

**Known:** YES for non-bipartite families (Erdős-Stone). A folklore counterexample exists for infinite families.

**Status:** OPEN for general finite families containing bipartite graphs.
mathContext: The Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(n; \mathcal{F})$ counts the maximum edges in an $n$-vertex graph that avoids every member of $\mathcal{F}$ as a subgraph. The **domination question** asks: is $\mathrm{ex}(n; \mathcal{F})$ always asymptotically determined by a single member $G \in \mathcal{F}$, in the sense that $\mathrm{ex}(n; G) = O(\mathrm{ex}(n; \mathcal{F}))$? This is a fundamental structural question about extremal functions.

title: Turán Numbers and Domination
content:
**turanNumber H n:** The supremum of edge counts in $n$-vertex $H$-free graphs, defined via `sSup`.

**ExSingle, ExFamily:** Type aliases for $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, representing extremal functions for single graphs and families.

**HasDomination familyEx memberExs:** $\exists\, g \in \text{memberExs},\, \exists\, C > 0,\, \forall\, n:\, g(n) \leq C \cdot \text{familyEx}(n)$. This formalizes the Big-$O$ relation $\mathrm{ex}(n; G) = O(\mathrm{ex}(n; \mathcal{F}))$.
mathContext: The `sSup` definition of `turanNumber` takes $\sup\{m : \exists G\text{ on Fin } n,\, H(G) \wedge |E(G)| = m\}$. Edges are counted via filtering ordered pairs $(i,j)$ with $i < j$ and $G.\text{Adj}\, i\, j$ from `Finset.univ`. The abstract $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ representation avoids encoding specific graph structures, focusing on the growth rate of the extremal function.

title: Main Conjecture (OPEN)
content:
**ErdosConjecture180:** Every finite nonempty family has the domination property.

Formalized as: $\forall$ familyEx memberExs, memberExs.Nonempty $\to$ ($\forall n$, familyEx $n \leq$ inf' memberExs) $\to$ HasDomination familyEx memberExs.

This is the precise formalization of Erdős Problem #180. No axiom is provided — it remains OPEN.
mathContext: The conjecture is stated as a `Prop` (not an axiom), reflecting its open status. The hypothesis $\mathrm{familyEx}(n) \leq \inf'(\text{memberExs})$ ensures consistency: the family Turán number cannot exceed the minimum of individual members' Turán numbers. The `Finset.inf'` requires nonemptiness, formalized via `memberExs.Nonempty`. Note the conjecture quantifies over abstract extremal functions, not over concrete graph families — a design choice that simplifies the formalization.

title: Non-Bipartite Case (Erdős-Stone)
content:
**axiom erdos_stone_domination:** For non-bipartite families, the Erdős-Stone theorem gives $\mathrm{ex}(n; H) = \left(\frac{r-2}{r-1} + o(1)\right)\binom{n}{2}$ where $r = \chi(H)$ is the chromatic number. The member with smallest chromatic number dominates the family.

Axiomatized because the full Erdős-Stone theorem and its asymptotic analysis are beyond current Mathlib.
mathContext: The **Erdős-Stone theorem** (1946) is one of the most important results in extremal graph theory: $\mathrm{ex}(n; H) = \left(1 - \frac{1}{\chi(H)-1} + o(1)\right)\frac{n^2}{2}$. For non-bipartite $H$ ($\chi(H) \geq 3$), this determines $\mathrm{ex}(n; H)$ up to $o(n^2)$, so the member with minimal $\chi$ dominates. The theorem fails to distinguish bipartite graphs ($\chi = 2$) since all give $\mathrm{ex}(n; H) = o(n^2)$. Note: the axiom is stated more strongly than needed — it asserts domination for all families, not just non-bipartite ones.

title: Bipartite Case and Counterexamples
content:
**BipartiteCase:** The negation of the conjecture — existence of a finite family without domination. Defined as a `Prop` to potentially serve as a refutation target.

**folklore_counterexample_infinite:** For infinite families, domination fails. Example: $\mathcal{F} = \{K_{1,n} : n \geq 1\} \cup \{nK_2 : n \geq 1\}$ (stars + matchings) gives $\mathrm{ex}(n; \mathcal{F}) = O(1)$ but each individual member allows $\Theta(n)$ edges.
mathContext: For bipartite $H$, the Erdős-Stone theorem gives only $\mathrm{ex}(n; H) = o(n^2)$, and precise asymptotics depend on the **Zarankiewicz problem**: $\mathrm{ex}(n; K_{s,t}) = O(n^{2-1/s})$ by the Kővári-Sós-Turán theorem. Different bipartite graphs have different polynomial growth rates within $o(n^2)$, making the domination question subtle. The folklore counterexample axiom formalizes: $\exists$ familyEx memberExs such that $\mathrm{familyEx}(n) \leq 1$ for all $n$, yet every member $g$ grows unboundedly ($\forall C,\, \exists n,\, g(n) > C$).

title: Family Monotonicity
content: **axiom family_le_members:** $\mathrm{ex}(n; \mathcal{F}) \leq \min_{G \in \mathcal{F}} \mathrm{ex}(n; G)$. Forbidding more subgraphs can only reduce the maximum edge count, since any $\mathcal{F}$-free graph is also $G$-free for each $G \in \mathcal{F}$.
mathContext: This is a fundamental monotonicity property: if $\mathcal{F} \supseteq \{G\}$, then $\mathrm{ex}(n; \mathcal{F}) \leq \mathrm{ex}(n; G)$ because the feasible set of $\mathcal{F}$-free graphs is contained in the set of $G$-free graphs. Taking the minimum over all $G \in \mathcal{F}$ gives $\mathrm{ex}(n; \mathcal{F}) \leq \min_{G \in \mathcal{F}} \mathrm{ex}(n; G)$. Axiomatized via `Finset.inf'` which requires the nonemptiness witness.

title: Summary Theorem
content:
**theorem erdos_180_summary:** Proves the conjunction of:
1. Non-bipartite domination (from `erdos_stone_domination`)
2. Infinite family counterexample (from `folklore_counterexample_infinite`)

The proof is a one-liner: `exact ⟨erdos_stone_domination, folklore_counterexample_infinite⟩`. The OPEN question is whether domination holds for ALL finite families, especially those containing bipartite graphs.
mathContext: The summary captures the complete state of knowledge as a single Lean `theorem`: the non-bipartite case is resolved ($\wedge$ left conjunct) and finiteness is essential ($\wedge$ right conjunct). The gap between these two results — finite families containing bipartite graphs — is the open problem. The proof is trivial (`exact ⟨_, _⟩`) because both halves are axioms.
